s:
c. 973, Æthelwold, translation of the Rule of Saint Benedict
Hīe habbaþ sīde earmellan and pohhode hosan.
They have wide sleeves and baggy pants.

y: From Proto-West Germanic *hosp, *husp (“derision, mockery”), of obscure origin. Likely an alteration of Proto-West Germanic *hosk, *husk (“derision, mockery”), from Proto-Germanic *huskaz, *huską (“mockery”), from Proto-Indo-European *kūd- (“to shout, be naughty, mock”). More at Old English husc.
From Proto-West Germanic *hosā, from Proto-Germanic *husǭ, *hausaz (“covering, shell, leggings”).

s: gorge; a narrow outlet at the upper end of a valley
y: From Proto-West Germanic *hrakō, from Proto-Indo-European *kreg- (“to caw, crow”).

Se underling, sum wīdcūð cræftiga georn godwīsdōmes and dēofolcræftes, wearð ellenwōd on þǣre tīde þæs hramman Wilcoxes geongan
The subject, a widely known architect with leanings toward theosophy and occultism, went violently insane on the date of young Wilcox’s seizure
y: From Proto-Germanic *hramjō, related to hremman, Old Norse hremma and Old Dutch *remmen from Proto-Germanic *hramjaną (“to hinder, clutch”). Possibly cognate with Old Norse hrammr (“bear claw”) (from Proto-Germanic *hramjaz (“clutching”)).

s: garlic, ramsons, wild garlic, Allium ursinum
a small whale or large delphinid
7~8th c., Glossa in Psalmos; Vatican Library MS. Pal. lat. 68, folio 12v
... seven fish fill a seal, seven seals fill a "hran", seven "hrans" fill a whale.
y: Origin unknown, cf. Épinal Glossary hran (c. 700) and Futhorc ᚻᚱᚩᚾᚫᛋ (hrónæs) (gen. sg.) on the Franks Casket (early 8th c.). Perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *harzaz (“a kind of fish”). Compare Norwegian harr (“grayling”), Swedish harr (“grayling”).

s:
late 9th century, translation of Orosius’ History Against the Pagans
Þā dēor hī hātaþ hrānas...
y: Calque of Old Norse hreinn, as if from Proto-West Germanic *hrain, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hrainaz. At the time, Old Norse and Old English were sufficiently close that the correspondence between ā and ei was transparent, as in words like stān (“stone”) and steinn (“id.”).

s: The meaning of this term is uncertain. Possibilities include
the two of us meant to protect ourselves from sharks(?).
a large predatory fish, such as a shark

y: Kenning of hran (“small whale or large delphinid”) + rād (“riding”).

From Proto-West Germanic *hratalā, from Proto-Germanic *hrat- (“to rattle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerd- (“to move, swing, jump”). Cognate with Middle Dutch ratele, ratel, whence Dutch ratel, ratelaar.

From Proto-West Germanic *hratōn, from Proto-Germanic *hratōną (“to sway, reel, stagger, stumble”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerd- (“to move, swing, jump”). Cognate with Old Norse hrata (“to fall, tumble, stagger, rush”). Compare similar yet unrelated Old English hraþian, hradian (“to quicken, hasten”).

s: ᛠ byþ eġle eorla ġehwylċum þon fæstlīċe flǣsċ onġinnaþ hrāw...
The grave is grim to every nobleman When quickly begins the flesh, The corpse...
"Take your only-begotten son Isaac, whom you love, and quickly go to the land of Visionis, and sacrifice him there upon a mountain."

c. 900, Werferth, translation of the Dialogues of Gregory
Sume nihte, þā þā hē wel ǣr ārās tō bētenne þā lēoht þe wǣron nēah þǣre dura, and þā stōd hē on triewenre hlǣdre under þām lēohtfæte and ontende and ġebētte þæt lēoht, þā stōd þǣr ofdūne on þǣre flōre sanctus Petrus sē ēadega apostol on hwītum hræġlum, and þus cwæþ tō him, "Þū ġefēra, for hwon ārise þū swā hraðe?"

One night, when he had gotten up very early to kindle the lights near the door, and he was standing on a wooden ladder under the lamp to light the fire, down on the floor stood Saint Peter the apostle dressed in white, and he said to him, "Comrade, why did you get up so early?"
y: From Proto-West Germanic *hraþē or *hraþō ~ *hradō (“quickly”), equivalent to hræd + -e.

superlative degree of hraþe; fastest, earliest

y: From Proto-West Germanic *hrawō, from Proto-West Germanic *hrau (“raw”). Compare Icelandic hrái (“rawness”).

y: From Proto-Germanic *hraukaz. Cognate with West Frisian reak, Middle Dutch rooc (Dutch rook), Old Norse hraukr.

y:
Origin obscure. Perhaps from Proto-West Germanic *hraþamūs (literally “fleet-mouse, swift-mouse”), equivalent to hræd + mūs. Compare Old Saxon hradamūs (“bat”), Old High German rodamūs (“bat”).
Alternatively, first element from Proto-Indo-European *krew- (“to shake, wave around”), related to Tocharian A kru (“reed”), Tocharian B kärwats, Lithuanian krutéti (“to move”); second element from mūs (“mouse”).

s:
c. 995, Ælfric, Homilies, "On the Holy Day of Pentecost"
... forðan ðe God hī hredde wið heora fȳnd, ...
... because God had saved them from their enemies, ...
y: From Proto-West Germanic *hraddjan, from Proto-Germanic *hradjaną (“to save, rescue”). Akin to Old Frisian hredda, Old High German *retten (German retten).

Martinus ġelācnode mid ǣnlīpium cosse ǣnne hrēoflīnne mannan fram his micclan coðe, and fram atelīcum hīwe his unsmēðan līċes.
Martinus cured a leprous man of his great sickness and from the horrid appearance of his unsmooth body with a single kiss.

Exeter Book, The Wanderer
Ne mæg werig mod · wyrde wiðstondan,
ne se hreo hyge · helpe gefremman.
A weary mind cannot withstand fate,
nor the worried mind help out.
y: From Proto-Germanic *hreuhaz (“bad, wild”), from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“raw meat, fresh blood”).

Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church
...ðā ðā hǣðenan āhēowon þæt trēow mid ormǣtre blisse, þæt hit brastliende sāh tō ðām hālgan were, hetelīċe swīðe. Þā worhte hē onġēan ðām hrēosendum trēowe þǣs Hǣlendes rōde tācn, and hit ðǣrrihte ætstōd, wende ðā onġēan, and hrēas underbæc, and fornēan offēoll ðā ðe hit ǣr forcurfon.

Then the heathens cut down the tree with great joy, so that, rustling, it fell towards the holy man very violently. Then he made the sign of the Savior's cross to the falling tree, and it immediately stood still, turned around, and fell down backwards, and almost fell upon those who had previously cut it.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *hreusan, from Proto-Germanic *hreusaną (“to fall down”). Cognate with Old High German riosan.

s:
c. 992, Ælfric, "THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THE LORD'S EPIPHANY"
Mihtiglice he mihte mid his worde hine gehælan, buton hrepunge; ac he geswutelode þæt his hrepung is swiðe halwende geleaffullum.
In his might he could have healed him with his word, without touching; but he manifested that his touch is very salutary to believers.
Crist mid his handa hrepunge þone hreoflian gehælde, swa eac he alysde us fram ure sawla synnum ðurh anfenge ures flæsces; swa swa se witega Isaias cwæð, "Soðlice he sylf ætbræd ure adlunga, and ure sarnyssa he sylf abær."

Christ by the touch of his hands healed the leper, so also he redeemed us from the sins of our souls by the assumption of our flesh; as the prophet Isaiah said, "Verily he took away our diseases, and our pains he himself bare."
the sense of touch (one of the five senses)

c. 992, Ælfric, "ON THE PURIFICATION OF ST. MARY"
Ure yfelan geðohtas oððe weorc we sceolan alysan mid fif scyllingum; þæt is we sceolon ure yfelnysse behreowsian mid urum fif andgitum, þæt synd gesihþ, and hlyst, and swæc, and stenc, and hrepung.
Our evil thoughts or actions we should redeem with five shillings; that is, we should repent of our wickedness with our five senses, which are, sight, and hearing, and taste, and smell, and touch.

rare; not thoroughly cooked; (of eggs) lightly boiled

Oft him ānhaga · āre gebīdeð,
Metudes miltse, · þēah þe hē mōdċeariġ
ġeond lagulāde · longe sċeolde
hrēran mid hondum · hrīmċealde sǣ,
wadan wræclāstas. · Wyrd bið ful ārǣd.

A loner oft waits a grace for himself,
Creator's mercy, even if he is sorrowful,
through a sea-way he should for long
stir the frost-cold sea with hands,
travel paths of exile. Fate is well stalwart.

y: From hrēr (adjective), from hrēran (“to move quickly”). Equivalent to hrēr + -e.

y: From Proto-Germanic *hrōþiz. Cognate with Old High German *hruod (used in personal names), Old Norse hróðr.
From Proto-Germanic *Hrōþijǭ, related to *hrōþiz (“fame, glory”). Cognate with Old High German *Hrouda, Hruada.

s: Hrethel, a king of the Geats mentioned in Beowulf

Beorn sċeal ġebīdan, · þonne hē bēot spriceð,
oþþæt collenferð · cunne ġearwe
hwider hreþra ġehyġd · hweorfan wille.

Man must pause when he tells a promise
until bold spirit would know clearly
where thought of hearts would turn.

Forþon nū mīn hyġe hweorfeð ofer hreþerlocan; mīn mōdsefa mid mereflōde ofer hwæles ēþel hweorfeð wīde, eorþan sċēatas, cymeð eft tō mē ġīfre ond grǣdiġ; ġielleð ānfloga, hweteð on wæl weġ hreþer unwearnum ofer holma ġelagu.

Thus, my mind now wanders over heartstead; my soul wanders afar with the sea-flood over whale’s home, on the Earth’s corners, comes back, greedy and hungry, to me; the lone-flyer yells, whets the soul on the slain way over the stretch of waters with no refuses.

y: From Proto-Germanic *hrōþīgaz. Equivalent to hrēþ + -iġ. Cognate with Gothic *𐌷𐍂𐍉𐌸𐍃 (*hrōþs) (used in personal names), 𐌷𐍂𐍉𐌸𐌴𐌹𐌲𐍃 (hrōþeigs).

s: a member of the Geatish royal house in the poem Beowulf; a descendant of King Hreþel
y: By surface analysis, Hreþel (a name) + -ing (“descendant of”)

s: the third month of the year according to the Anglo-Saxon calendar
y: From *Hrēþe + mōnaþ. Alternatively, from hrēþ + mōnaþ
From Proto-West Germanic *hrīdrā, from Proto-Germanic *hrīdrą, *hrīdrǭ (“sieve”), from Proto-Germanic *hrid- (“to shake”), from Proto-Indo-European *krey-.

s:
late 10th c., Ælfric of Eynsham, "The Passion of St. Bartholomew the Apostle"
Sē lǣċe ċierfþ oþþe bærnþ, and sē untruma hrīemþ, þēah hwæðre ne miltsaþ hē þæs ōðres wānunge, for þon þe ġif sē lǣċe ġeswīcþ his cræftes, þonne losaþ sē forwunoda.
The surgeon cuts or burns, and the patient screams, yet the surgeon doesn't give in to the patient's cries, because if he lets up from his task, the patient will die.
y: From Proto-Germanic *hraumijan, derived from *hraum, whence Old English hrēam.
